def: An act of gambling money; or a risky action undertaken in the hope of success.
ex: Launching a new mobile app without preliminary user testing is a dangerous commercial gamble.
nat: He took a gamble by leaving his corporate job to launch an independent startup.

mis.bad: Investing in crypto was a big gamble of him.
mis.good: Investing in crypto was a big gamble for him.
mis.why: Use "gamble for someone", not "of him".

def: To gather or collect something, especially information, support, or approval.
ex: The open-source developer managed to garner widespread international praise for creating the security tool.
nat: Her proposal garnered substantial financial support from local angel investors.

mis.bad: The project garnered to many positive reviews.
mis.good: The project garnered many positive reviews.
mis.why: "Garner" is a transitive verb; do not add "to" after it.

def: A body of troops stationed in a fortress or town to defend it.
ex: A military garrison was stationed near the international mountain border to maintain regional peace.
nat: The historic fortress housed an infantry garrison of six hundred soldiers during wartime.

mis.bad: The soldiers were in the garrison of the city.
mis.good: The soldiers were stationed at the garrison.
mis.why: Collocate "stationed at a garrison", not "in the garrison of".

pt: ofegar / abrir a boca de espanto
def: To inhale suddenly and sharply with an open mouth, typically through surprise or pain.
ex: The audience gasped in astonishment when the magician made the grand piano vanish completely.
nat: He gasped for breath after sprinting up four flights of concrete stairs.

mis.bad: She gasped with shock at the news.
mis.good: She gasped in shock at the news.
mis.why: Say "gasped in shock" or "gasped in surprise", using "in".

def: To look steadily and intently, especially in admiration, surprise, or deep thought.
ex: We sat on the hotel balcony and gazed at the quiet Mediterranean sunset together.
nat: She gazed into the distance, pondering the difficult career choice ahead.

mis.bad: He gazed to the stars for hours.
mis.good: He gazed at the stars for hours.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "at" after "gaze": "gaze at something".

def: To produce or create something such as electricity, revenue, ideas, or files.
ex: The solar panel installation will generate clean renewable energy for more than fifty households.
nat: The promotional campaign generated thousands of qualified sales leads in two weeks.

mis.bad: The campaign generated to many new clients.
mis.good: The campaign generated many new clients.
mis.why: "Generate" is transitive; do not use "to" after the verb.

def: A machine or device that converts mechanical energy into electricity, or creates code.
ex: The hospital switched to a diesel emergency generator within seconds of the power failure.
nat: Modern web frameworks provide a command-line code generator to create basic database schemas.

mis.bad: The hospital has a generator of energy.
mis.good: The hospital has a backup generator / power generator.
mis.why: Use compound nouns like "power generator" or "backup generator" rather than "generator of energy".

def: Characteristic of or relating to a class or group of things; not specific.
ex: Buying generic medication at the pharmacy provides the same active ingredients at lower cost.
nat: The rejection email was completely generic and contained no personalized feedback on my interview.

mis.bad: This medicine is a generic one.
mis.good: This medicine is a generic drug / generic.
mis.why: Avoid adding redundant "one" after "generic"; say "is generic" or "is a generic drug".

def: The quality of being kind and plentiful in giving money or time.
ex: The disaster relief organization thanked donors for their extraordinary generosity after the earthquake.
nat: Her hospitality and natural generosity made all international visitors feel immediately welcome.

mis.bad: He thanked me for my generosity with him.
mis.good: He thanked me for my generosity toward him.
mis.why: Use "generosity toward/to someone", not "with him".

def: Exceptional intellectual or creative power or other natural ability; or such a person.
ex: Albert Einstein is widely recognized as a scientific genius who reshaped modern physics completely.
nat: Her true genius lies in translating complex algorithmic concepts into simple visual diagrams.

mis.bad: He is an absolute genius in mathematics.
mis.good: He is an absolute genius at / in mathematics.
mis.why: Say "a genius at" when referring to skills (coding, math, chess).

def: A category of artistic, musical, or literary composition characterized by a particular style.
ex: Science fiction has always been my favorite literary genre since early middle school.
nat: Streaming platforms use machine learning algorithms to recommend content across various music genres.

mis.bad: What is your favorite book gender?
mis.good: What is your favorite book genre?
mis.why: False friend! "Gender" refers to male/female identity; "genre" (/ˈʒɑːnrə/) refers to artistic or literary category.

def: A microorganism, especially one that causes disease; or the initial stage of an idea.
ex: Washing your hands with warm water and soap eliminates germs that cause seasonal flu.
nat: That brief corridor conversation was the initial germ of our million-dollar product idea.

mis.bad: Wash hands to avoid the microbials.
mis.good: Wash your hands to kill germs / avoid germs.
mis.why: Use common word "germs" rather than technical "microbials" in everyday English.

pt: germinar / começar a brotar ou surgir
def: To begin to grow and put out shoots after a period of dormancy.
ex: Tomato seeds need warm moist soil and sunlight in order to germinate properly indoors.
nat: The ambitious business idea began to germinate while the two friends were traveling abroad.

mis.bad: The seeds germinated out after five days.
mis.good: The seeds germinated after five days.
mis.why: Do not add "out" after "germinate".

def: Of very great size or extent; huge or colossal.
ex: The tech corporation built a gigantic data center powered entirely by nearby hydroelectric plants.
nat: She faced a gigantic pile of unread emails after returning from two weeks away.

mis.bad: It was a gigantic big problem for us.
mis.good: It was a gigantic problem for us.
mis.why: "Gigantic" already means very big; never combine it with "big".

def: To laugh lightly and repeatedly in a silly or nervous way.
ex: The young children could not stop giggling during the funny puppet show performance.
nat: She giggled nervously when asked to give an impromptu speech to the team.

mis.bad: They were giving giggles at the back.
mis.good: They were giggling at the back of the room.
mis.why: Use the verb "giggle" directly rather than "giving giggles".

def: The substance or general meaning of a speech or text; the essence.
ex: Even if you miss a few vocabulary words, try to catch the overall gist.
nat: Can you give me the gist of the client meeting in two sentences?

mis.bad: I understood the gist of the discussion about.
mis.good: I understood the gist of the discussion.
mis.why: Do not leave a dangling "about"; say "the gist of [something]".

def: Having glamour; excitingly attractive and charming, often superficially so.
ex: Working in fashion sounds glamorous, but the daily reality involves long hours and heavy lifting.
nat: The film festival opened with a glamorous red-carpet ceremony attended by international celebrities.

mis.bad: She dressed very glamorous for the gala.
mis.good: She dressed very glamorously for the gala.
mis.why: Use the adverb "glamorously" to modify the verb "dressed".

def: A brief or hurried look.
ex: A quick glance at the dashboard confirmed that all microservices were running healthy today.
nat: She cast a nervous glance toward the exit before beginning her presentation.

mis.bad: In a glance, I saw the error in code.
mis.good: At a glance, I saw the error in the code.
mis.why: The correct fixed idiom is "at a glance", not "in a glance".

def: To stare in an angry or fierce way, or shine with strong dazzling light.
ex: The midday tropical sun glared relentlessly down on the open agricultural fields all afternoon.
nat: The commuter glared at the passenger who was talking loudly on speakerphone.

mis.bad: He glared to me with anger.
mis.good: He glared at me in anger.
mis.why: Always use "glare at [someone]", not "to".

def: To shine brightly, especially with reflected light; glimmer.
ex: Her eyes gleamed with excitement when she opened the acceptance letter from Stanford.
nat: The newly waxed hardwood floors gleamed in the soft morning sunlight.

mis.bad: His eyes gleamed of happiness.
mis.good: His eyes gleamed with happiness.
mis.why: Collocate "gleam with [an emotion]" (excitement, pride, happiness), using "with".

def: To move with a smooth, continuous, and effortless motion.
ex: Ice skaters glide effortlessly across the frozen pond under the crisp winter sky.
nat: The large eagle spread its wings and glided silently over the green valley.

mis.bad: The swans glided on top the lake.
mis.good: The swans glided across the lake.
mis.why: Use "glide across" or "glide over" for smooth motion.

def: A momentary or partial view of someone or something.
ex: Fans waited outside the concert arena for hours hoping to catch a glimpse of the singer.
nat: The documentary gave viewers a fascinating glimpse into life aboard the International Space Station.

mis.bad: I had a glimpse at him yesterday.
mis.good: I caught a glimpse of him yesterday.
mis.why: The natural idiomatic verb phrase is "catch a glimpse of", not "have a glimpse at".

def: To shine with a sparkling light, especially from a wet or oily surface.
ex: Morning dew caused the emerald grass blades to glisten brightly in the early sunshine.
nat: Sweat glistened on the marathon runner's forehead as she approached the finish line.

mis.bad: The streets glistened of rain.
mis.good: The streets glistened with rain.
mis.why: Use the preposition "with" with "glisten": "glisten with rain / sweat / dew".

def: Relating to the whole world; worldwide; or comprehensive.
ex: Climate change is an urgent global challenge that requires unprecedented international diplomatic cooperation.
nat: The technology company has established global headquarters in Singapore and offices in London.

mis.bad: We work in a global scale company.
mis.good: We work on a global scale / for a global company.
mis.why: Say "on a global scale" with preposition "on".

def: To praise or worship something; or make something appear more splendid than it is.
ex: Action video games are often criticized for glorifying reckless violence to impressionable teenagers.
nat: The historic monument was constructed to glorify the nation's naval victories.

mis.bad: The movie glorifies about criminal lifestyle.
mis.good: The movie glorifies the criminal lifestyle.
mis.why: "Glorify" is transitive; do not insert "about" after the verb.

def: Shiny and smooth; or superficially attractive and stylish.
ex: The marketing agency printed the new product brochures on premium glossy paper for distributors.
nat: The horse had a beautiful glossy black coat that shone under the sun.

mis.bad: We chose a glossy finish paint.
mis.good: We chose paint with a glossy finish.
mis.why: Collocate "with a glossy finish" or "glossy paint".

def: To give out steady light without a flame; or look healthy and warm.
ex: The neon sign continued to glow softly through the thick evening city fog.
nat: Her face glowed with pride as she accepted the university diploma on stage.

mis.bad: The toy glows on the dark.
mis.good: The toy glows in the dark.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "glows in the dark", using "in".

def: Having or showing grace or elegance in movement, shape, or behavior.
ex: The ballerina performed a graceful pirouette across the polished wooden theater stage.
nat: She gave a graceful concession speech after the election results were officially certified.

mis.bad: The dancer moved very graceful.
mis.good: The dancer moved very gracefully.
mis.why: Modify the verb with the adverb "gracefully".

def: An inclined part of a road or railway; or a rate of change of a variable.
ex: Cyclists struggled to maintain speed on the steep gradient leading up the mountain pass.
nat: Deep learning models use gradient descent algorithms to minimize error during model training.

mis.bad: The road has a steep incline gradient.
mis.good: The road has a steep gradient.
mis.why: Do not say "incline gradient"; "gradient" already signifies the degree of incline or slope.

pt: grão (cereal ou areia) / textura de madeira
def: Wheat or other cultivated cereal fruit; or a single small particle of something.
ex: Whole grain bread provides long-lasting energy and essential B vitamins for busy mornings.
nat: Always sand the wooden tabletop along the natural grain rather than against it.

mis.bad: Eat more whole grains for your diet.
mis.good: Eat more whole grain foods / whole grains.
mis.why: When referring to crops, "grain" is often singular or used in compounds like "whole grain".

def: Magnificent and imposing in appearance, size, or style.
ex: The international delegates attended a grand banquet inside the historic municipal palace last night.
nat: They unveiled a grand plan to transition the entire public bus fleet to electric.

mis.bad: The house was very grandious inside.
mis.good: The house was very grand / grandiose inside.
mis.why: "Grand" is standard for magnificent; "grandiose" often implies pretentious or excessively ambitious.

def: Impressive and imposing in appearance or style, especially pretentiously so.
ex: The bankrupt startup founder had grandiose ambitions but failed to execute even basic features.
nat: The architectural proposal was criticized as overly grandiose for such a quiet residential district.

mis.bad: He has grandiose ideas about his future (compliment).
mis.good: He has ambitious / great ideas about his future.
mis.why: In English, "grandiose" almost always carries a negative connotation of being unrealistically pretentious.

def: To agree to give or allow something requested; or admit to be true.
ex: The university decided to grant her a full academic scholarship for graduate study.
nat: The immigration department granted him a temporary residency visa after thorough review.

mis.bad: The system granted the access for me.
mis.good: The system granted me access.
mis.why: Use the double-object pattern: "grant [someone] [something]" or "grant [something] to [someone]".

def: Relating to visual art, especially drawing or engraving; or giving clear, vivid detail.
ex: The news report issued a trigger warning before showing graphic images of the earthquake damage.
nat: She works as a graphic designer specializing in user interface typography and branding.

mis.bad: The documentary gave a graphic description of the battle.
mis.good: The documentary gave a vivid / graphic description of the battle.
mis.why: "Graphic" often implies uncomfortably vivid or gory details when used with "description".

def: To engage in a close fight or struggle without weapons; or struggle to deal with.
ex: Cities around the world must grapple with housing affordability and rising public transit costs.
nat: The engineering team is grappling with how to reduce API response latency under heavy load.

mis.bad: The team is grappling about the budget.
mis.good: The team is grappling with the budget issues.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "with" with "grapple": "grapple with a problem".

def: To seize and hold firmly, or fully understand the meaning of something complex.
ex: It took several weeks of practical exercises to fully grasp the concepts behind distributed computing.
nat: She grasped the railing firmly as the ferry rolled across the choppy waves.

mis.bad: He failed to grasp of the importance of security.
mis.good: He failed to grasp the importance of security.
mis.why: "Grasp" is transitive; do not insert "of" after the verb.

def: The quality of being thankful; readiness to show appreciation for kindness received.
ex: The team expressed deep gratitude to their mentor for her patient guidance during the hackathon.
nat: Writing in a daily journal is an effective way to cultivate heartfelt gratitude.

mis.bad: I want to express my gratitude for you.
mis.good: I want to express my gratitude to you.
mis.why: Express gratitude "to" someone, and "for" a gift or favor: "gratitude to you for your help".

def: Giving cause for alarm; serious or solemn in character or manner.
ex: The medical team expressed grave concern regarding the rapid spread of the respiratory virus.
nat: He looked grave as he delivered the news of the company's quarterly losses.

mis.bad: This is a grave error for the system.
mis.good: This is a grave / serious error in the system.
mis.why: "Grave" describes heavy, critical situations; collocate with "danger", "concern", or "consequences".

def: To eat grass in a field, or scrape and break the surface of the skin.
ex: Dairy cows grazed peacefully on the lush green hillsides outside the quiet alpine village.
nat: The falling rock grazed his shoulder, leaving only a minor superficial scratch.

mis.bad: He grazed his knee on the wall.
mis.good: He grazed his knee against the wall.
mis.why: Say "grazed his knee against the wall" or "on the asphalt".

def: Thick oily animal fat or semi-solid lubricant used for machinery parts.
ex: The bicycle mechanic applied fresh waterproof grease to the wheel bearings before reassembling the hub.
nat: Dish soap helps cut through tough bacon grease on non-stick frying pans.

mis.bad: Clean the grease of the engine.
mis.good: Clean the grease from the engine.
mis.why: Use "clean grease from / off something", not "of".

def: To give a polite word or sign of welcome or recognition to someone.
ex: The conference organizers greeted international attendees at the registration desk with welcome bags.
nat: She greeted her former professor with a warm smile and a polite handshake.

mis.bad: He greeted to everyone when entering.
mis.good: He greeted everyone when entering the room.
mis.why: "Greet" is transitive; do not use "to" before the person.

def: Very serious or gloomy; depressing or uninviting in outlook.
ex: The economic forecast painted a grim picture for small retailers over the coming winter.
nat: Firefighters faced grim working conditions inside the smoke-filled industrial warehouse.

mis.bad: The situation was in a grim state.
mis.good: The situation was grim / looked grim.
mis.why: Use the adjective predicate "was grim" directly.

def: To smile broadly, especially so as to show one's teeth.
ex: He could not help grinning from ear to ear after passing his driving exam.
nat: She grinned mischievously as she revealed the surprise birthday cake to the team.

mis.bad: He gave a grin smile to me.
mis.good: He gave me a broad grin / smiled broadly.
mis.why: Do not say "grin smile"; "grin" is already a broad smile.

def: To crush into small particles between hard surfaces; or work relentlessly.
ex: It is best to grind fresh coffee beans immediately before brewing for maximum aromatic flavor.
nat: Many tech professionals grind long hours for years hoping for a successful startup exit.

mis.bad: He grinded the beans this morning.
mis.good: He ground the beans this morning.
mis.why: Irregular past tense: grind — ground — ground.

def: A firm hold on something; or an understanding and control over a situation.
ex: Winter tires provide superior road grip when driving on icy, snow-covered highway surfaces.
nat: The company is slowly losing its grip on the domestic smartphone market.

mis.bad: Keep a firm grip in the handle.
mis.good: Keep a firm grip on the handle.
mis.why: Use the preposition "on": "a grip on something".

def: Courage and resolve; strength of character; or small coarse particles of sand or stone.
ex: Succeeding in a demanding startup environment requires exceptional intelligence combined with relentless personal grit.
nat: Road crews spread salt and grit across icy city streets before the freezing morning rush.

mis.bad: He has much grit for to succeed.
mis.good: He showed tremendous grit to succeed.
mis.why: Use "show grit" or "have grit", followed by an infinitive.

def: To make a deep inarticulate sound in response to pain or despair.
ex: The entire office groaned audibly when the manager announced another mandatory Saturday morning workshop.
nat: He groaned in pain as the physiotherapist massaged his injured lower back muscle.

mis.bad: The audience groaned about the delay.
mis.good: The audience groaned at the news of the delay.
mis.why: Collocate "groan at [news]" or "groan in [pain/frustration]".

def: A long, narrow cut or depression; or an established and comfortable routine.
ex: After two weeks of orientation, the new software intern finally got into the groove.
nat: Dirt had accumulated deep inside the silicone seal groove around the front door.

mis.bad: It took days to get back in the groove.
mis.good: It took days to get back into the groove.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "get into the groove" or "back into the groove".

def: Pioneering; innovative; introducing radical new concepts or methods.
ex: The research team published a groundbreaking paper on quantum error correction in leading physics journals.
nat: Her groundbreaking research on neural networks earned her the prestigious international Turing Award.

mis.bad: The study was very revolutionary groundbreaking.
mis.good: The study was groundbreaking / truly groundbreaking.
mis.why: Do not combine "revolutionary" and "groundbreaking"; they are synonymous.

def: Not based on any good reason or factual evidence; baseless.
ex: Management reassured staff that circulating rumors of imminent office closures were completely groundless.
nat: Her initial fears about speaking English in public proved to be entirely groundless.

mis.bad: Those rumors are without ground.
mis.good: Those rumors are groundless / baseless.
mis.why: Say "are groundless" rather than the literal Portuguese "without ground".

def: A small group of trees, especially one producing nuts or fruit.
ex: We enjoyed a picnic beneath the shade of an ancient olive grove in Tuscany.
nat: The resort features peaceful walking trails through a fragrant citrus grove.

mis.bad: They walked through a grove of woods.
mis.good: They walked through an olive grove / a quiet grove.
mis.why: A "grove" is specifically a small cluster of trees; don't say "grove of woods".

def: To make a low guttural sound of anger, or rumble quietly.
ex: The guard dog began to growl menacingly when strangers approached the property gate.
nat: My stomach started to growl loudly during the quiet silence of the exam.

mis.bad: My stomach is shouting with hunger.
mis.good: My stomach is growling / rumbling with hunger.
mis.why: In English stomachs "growl" or "rumble", never "shout".

def: A persistent feeling of ill will or resentment resulting from a past insult or injury.
ex: Holding a bitter personal grudge against former colleagues will only harm your own career peace.
nat: She does not hold grudges and always forgives honest misunderstandings quickly.

mis.bad: He keeps a grudge with his former boss.
mis.good: He holds a grudge against his former boss.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "hold a grudge against someone", not "with".

def: Extremely tiring and demanding; arduous.
ex: Completing the grueling marathon through humid conditions pushed every runner to absolute physical exhaustion.
nat: The startup founders survived a grueling three-month fundraising tour across the country.

mis.bad: It was a grueling work to finish the report.
mis.good: It was grueling work to finish the report.
mis.why: "Work" is uncountable in English; omit "a" before "grueling work".

def: To complain about something in a bad-tempered but subdued way.
ex: Employees often grumble about bureaucratic expense report procedures, but they always comply eventually.
nat: He sat at his desk grumbling under his breath about the new policy.

mis.bad: He grumbled with the delay of the train.
mis.good: He grumbled about the delay of the train.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "about" with "grumble": "grumble about something".

def: Bad-tempered and irritable, especially in the morning or when tired.
ex: He is always slightly grumpy before drinking his first cup of dark roast coffee.
nat: Lack of restorative sleep made the toddler unusually grumpy throughout the afternoon.

mis.bad: He woke up very bad-humored today.
mis.good: He woke up very grumpy / in a bad mood today.
mis.why: Instead of literal "bad-humored", use "grumpy" or "in a bad mood".

def: To provide a formal assurance or promise, especially that certain conditions will be fulfilled.
ex: The manufacturer will guarantee all hardware components against manufacturing defects for two full years.
nat: I cannot guarantee that the server migration will finish before the weekend.

mis.bad: We guarantee of the quality of our service.
mis.good: We guarantee the quality of our service.
mis.why: "Guarantee" takes a direct object without "of".

def: A person who keeps watch or protects something; or a protective device.
ex: A security guard checked identification badges before admitting visitors into the data center.
nat: Always wear a protective wrist guard when learning to skateboard or rollerblade.

mis.bad: The security guard caught me in surprise.
mis.good: The security guard caught me off guard.
mis.why: The idiom is "catch someone off guard" (pegar de surpresa).

def: A defender, protector, or keeper; or a person legally responsible for a minor.
ex: Parents or a legal guardian must sign the consent form before the school field trip.
nat: The constitutional court acts as the ultimate guardian of civil liberties and individual rights.

mis.bad: Her uncle is her legal guard.
mis.good: Her uncle is her legal guardian.
mis.why: Use "guardian" for legal custodian or protector of rights; "guard" is a physical security watchman.

def: Advice or information aimed at resolving a problem or difficulty, given by someone experienced.
ex: Under the expert guidance of senior developers, the interns deployed their first cloud microservice.
nat: Career guidance counseling helps high school students choose appropriate university degrees.

mis.bad: She gave me many good guidances for my career.
mis.good: She gave me a lot of good guidance / guidance for my career.
mis.why: "Guidance" is uncountable in English; do not say "many guidances".

def: To show the way to others, or direct the motion or positioning of something.
ex: An experienced mountain leader will guide our hiking group across the glacier safely.
nat: Mentors guide junior professionals through difficult career decisions and team negotiations.

mis.bad: He guided to the tourists around the city.
mis.good: He guided the tourists around the city.
mis.why: "Guide" is transitive; do not use "to" before the people being guided.

def: A general rule, principle, or piece of advice outlining best practices.
ex: The engineering organization established clear coding guidelines to ensure consistent architecture across all teams.
nat: Health authorities published strict dietary guidelines for managing high blood pressure.

mis.bad: We must follow the security guide lines.
mis.good: We must follow the security guidelines.
mis.why: "Guideline" (or "guidelines") is written as one single word.

def: The fact of having committed a specified or implied offense or crime; or the feeling of having done wrong.
ex: She felt an overwhelming sense of guilt after accidentally deleting her colleague's work.
nat: The jury reached a unanimous verdict of guilt after reviewing all evidence.

mis.bad: It was my guilt that the glasses broke.
mis.good: It was my fault that the glasses broke.
mis.why: Use "fault" for responsibility for an accident; use "guilt" for the moral remorse or legal culpability.

def: Easily persuaded to believe something; naive and easily tricked.
ex: Phishing scammers target gullible internet users who readily click on suspicious banking email links.
nat: He was too gullible to realize his friend was playing an elaborate practical joke.

mis.bad: He is very ingenuous to believe that scam.
mis.good: He is too gullible to believe that scam.
mis.why: False friend! English "ingenuous" means innocent/artless; someone who is easily duped is "gullible".

def: To swallow food or drink quickly or in large mouthfuls.
ex: The thirsty runner gulped down two full glasses of cold water immediately after finishing.
nat: He took a deep breath and gulped nervously before opening the exam envelope.

mis.bad: He gulped the water in one only sip.
mis.good: He gulped down the water in one single gulp.
mis.why: Use the phrasal verb "gulp down" and noun phrase "in one single gulp".

def: A brief, strong rush of wind.
ex: A sudden powerful gust of wind blew her umbrella inside out during the thunderstorm.
nat: Wind gusts of up to sixty miles per hour knocked down roadside power lines.

mis.bad: A big wind gust made the door close.
mis.good: A strong gust of wind blew the door shut.
mis.why: Say "a strong gust of wind" rather than "a big wind gust".

def: The stomach or intestines; or instinct and intuition; or courage.
ex: When choosing between two promising job offers, sometimes you must trust your gut.
nat: Fermented yogurt and kimchi help maintain a healthy, balanced gut microbiome balance.

mis.bad: I had a feeling in my stomach about the decision.
mis.good: I had a gut feeling about the decision.
mis.why: The natural English idiom for intuitive instinct is "gut feeling" or "trust your gut".

def: A shallow trough below the edge of a roof, or at the side of a street.
ex: Homeowners should clean dry fallen leaves out of roof gutters every autumn before rains.
nat: Rainwater rushed down the street gutter toward the municipal storm drain at high speed.

mis.bad: Water overflowed the roof calha.
mis.good: Water overflowed the roof gutter.
mis.why: The English word for a roof or street drainage channel is "gutter".

def: An item of clothing; a formal word for apparel or attire.
ex: Always read the washing instruction label stitched inside the garment to prevent fabric shrinkage.
nat: The local fashion boutique sells handcrafted organic cotton garments made by regional artisans.

mis.bad: I bought a new cloth yesterday.
mis.good: I bought a new garment / item of clothing yesterday.
mis.why: "Cloth" is the raw textile material; a specific item of clothing is a "garment" or "item of clothing".

pt: portal de acesso / portal de pagamento
def: An opening in a wall or fence; or a means of access to something.
ex: Our e-commerce checkout seamlessly connects to a secure international credit card payment gateway.
nat: Miami is often described as the commercial and cultural gateway to Latin America.

mis.bad: The country is a gateway for South America.
mis.good: The country is a gateway to South America.
mis.why: Use the preposition "to" after "gateway": "gateway to Latin America".

def: To acclaim or enthusiastically praise; or precipitate pellets of frozen rain.
ex: Critics across the globe hailed the indie video game as an artistic masterpiece of storytelling.
nat: Giant hailstones damaged parked cars throughout the city during the severe summer storm.

mis.bad: He hailed from Brazil in his speech.
mis.good: He hails from Brazil (meaning he is originally from Brazil).
mis.why: The idiom "hail from" means to originate from or be a native of a place.

def: A distinctive feature or characteristic of something, especially one indicating high quality.
ex: Clean, readable code with automated test coverage is the hallmark of a disciplined engineering organization.
nat: Meticulous attention to detail has always been the hallmark of Swiss watchmaking.

mis.bad: Attention to detail is a hallmark to great developers.
mis.good: Attention to detail is a hallmark of great developers.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "of" after "hallmark": "hallmark of something".

def: To bring or come to an abrupt stop.
ex: Management decided to halt construction on the new office tower pending environmental safety approvals.
nat: Train operations ground to a complete halt due to severe snowdrifts across the tracks.

mis.bad: The train made a halt in the station.
mis.good: The train came to a halt at the station.
mis.why: Use the idiom "come to a halt" or "brought to a halt", not "made a halt".

pt: reduzir pela metade / dividir em duas partes iguais
def: To divide into two equal parts, or reduce or decrease by half.
ex: Switching to cloud infrastructure allowed the e-commerce company to halve its monthly hosting expenditures.
nat: Halve the cherry tomatoes before tossing them into the fresh garden salad.

mis.bad: The company reduced by half its expenses (or "halved in half").
mis.good: The company halved its expenses.
mis.why: "Halve" already means reduce by half; do not say "halve in half" or "halve by half".

def: To hinder or impede the movement, progress, or development of someone or something.
ex: Heavy winter fog and icy runways continued to hamper flight operations at the busy international hub.
nat: A severe lack of budget funding will hamper scientific research into renewable solar batteries.

mis.bad: The rain hampered the team to finish the job.
mis.good: The rain hampered the team's progress / prevented the team from finishing.
mis.why: "Hamper" is transitive and takes a direct object (progress, efforts), not "hamper someone to do".

def: A quantity that fills the hand; or a small number of people or things.
ex: Only a small handful of senior engineers truly understand the entire legacy backend codebase.
nat: Grab a handful of roasted almonds from the pantry for an afternoon protein snack.

mis.bad: Only a handful of peoples attended the lecture.
mis.good: Only a handful of people attended the lecture.
mis.why: "People" is the irregular plural of "person"; never write "peoples" in this context.

def: Convenient to handle or use; useful; or placed close at hand.
ex: Keep a portable phone charger handy inside your carry-on bag during long international layovers.
nat: This keyboard shortcut reference sheet is extremely handy for junior software developers.

mis.bad: This tool will be very practice for us.
mis.good: This tool will be very handy / practical for us.
mis.why: False friend! In English, "practice" is a noun/verb; the adjective meaning useful and convenient is "handy" or "practical".

def: Lacking any obvious principle of organization; random and disorganized.
ex: Their haphazard approach to version control caused constant merge conflicts and lost code updates.
nat: Books were stacked in a haphazard pile beside the living room armchair.

mis.bad: The files were stored in a haphazardly way.
mis.good: The files were stored in a haphazard way / stored haphazardly.
mis.why: Use the adjective "haphazard" before "way" or the adverb "haphazardly" directly after the verb.

def: Unfortunate; having bad luck or unfortunate circumstances.
ex: The hapless tourist lost both his passport and wallet during his very first day in Rome.
nat: Customer support had to guide the hapless user through a simple password reset process.

mis.bad: He was very hapless with his investment.
mis.good: He was very unlucky with his investment / a hapless investor.
mis.why: "Hapless" is predominantly used as an attributive adjective before a noun: "hapless victim/tourist".

def: To keep a thought or feeling in mind; or give shelter to someone.
ex: Despite their past professional rivalry, she harbored no resentment toward her former business partner.
nat: Old damp buildings can harbor toxic black mold behind bathroom drywall panels.

mis.bad: He harbored doubts with the project success.
mis.good: He harbored doubts about the project's success.
mis.why: Collocate "harbor doubts about [something]", not "with".

def: Severe suffering or privation; conditions that make life very difficult.
ex: Refugee families endured severe economic hardship while waiting months for emergency settlement visas.
nat: He overcame tremendous personal hardship to become a leading physician and medical researcher.

mis.bad: They faced many hardships in their life (plural note).
mis.good: They faced severe hardship / many hardships in life.
mis.why: "Hardship" is commonly used uncountably to describe adversity or economic suffering.

def: Not able or likely to cause harm or damage.
ex: Most garden spiders found in the region are completely harmless to adult humans.
nat: It was just a harmless joke, but his colleague took offense immediately.

mis.bad: The snake is harmless for people.
mis.good: The snake is harmless to humans / people.
mis.why: Use the preposition "to" after "harmless": "harmless to someone".

def: To bring into agreement or harmony, or sing and make music in harmony.
ex: European nations worked together for years to harmonize cross-border corporate tax and tariff regulations.
nat: The choir singers harmonized beautifully during the opening hymn of the concert.

mis.bad: We need to harmonize our strategy to their vision.
mis.good: We need to harmonize our strategy with their vision.
mis.why: Use the preposition "with" with "harmonize": "harmonize A with B".

def: Unpleasantly rough or jarring to the senses; or cruel and severe.
ex: Arctic wildlife has adapted over millennia to survive the brutally harsh polar winter conditions.
nat: Her feedback was unexpectedly harsh, which discouraged the junior developer during code review.

mis.bad: The winter in Canada was very rude (meaning harsh).
mis.good: The winter in Canada was very harsh / severe.
mis.why: False friend! "Rude" means impolite; for severe weather or stern conditions, use "harsh" or "severe".

def: With excessive speed or urgency; hurriedly.
ex: The startup team hastily shipped a buggy patch without running standard automated integration tests.
nat: She packed her suitcase hastily and rushed to catch the early airport shuttle.

mis.bad: He hastily decided to quit without thinking.
mis.good: He made a hasty decision / decided hastily to quit.
mis.why: Use "hastily" to modify verbs; collocate "hastily assembled" or "hastily decided".

def: Done or acting with excessive speed or urgency; hurried and careless.
ex: Do not make a hasty decision about leaving your current job before securing another offer.
nat: After a hasty breakfast of toast and coffee, she hurried to the subway.

mis.bad: It was a precipitated decision to invest all our money.
mis.good: It was a hasty / rash decision to invest all our money.
mis.why: False friend! In English "precipitated" is not used for human choices; use "hasty" or "rash decision".

def: To emerge from an egg; or conspire to devise a secret plot or plan.
ex: Baby sea turtles hatch from sandy coastal nests and crawl instinctively toward the open ocean.
nat: The rival executives secretly hatched a plan to launch a competing cloud software venture.

mis.bad: The turtles born from the eggs on the beach.
mis.good: The turtles hatched from their eggs on the beach.
mis.why: Animals emerging from eggs "hatch", not "born".

def: To pull or drag with effort or force; or transport cargo in a truck.
ex: Heavy cargo freight trains haul thousands of tons of coal and grain across North America.
nat: He hauled the heavy wooden wardrobe up three flights of stairs without any elevator.

mis.bad: We had to pull the heavy luggage with effort.
mis.good: We had to haul the heavy luggage up the stairs.
mis.why: Use "haul" specifically when dragging or transporting heavy, bulky loads with great effort.

def: To manifest as a ghost; or cause repeated suffering or anxiety to a person.
ex: The painful memory of missing that crucial penalty kick continued to haunt him for years.
nat: Local legends claim that the spirit of an ancient sea captain haunts the rocky lighthouse.

mis.bad: The mistake haunted on him for months.
mis.good: The mistake haunted him for months.
mis.why: "Haunt" is a transitive verb; do not add "on" after it.

def: A place of safety or refuge; a harbor or small port for ships.
ex: The quiet public library was a welcome haven for students studying during intensive exam week.
nat: The offshore island has long served as a notorious tax haven for billionaire investors.

mis.bad: Switzerland is considered a fiscal paradise for investors.
mis.good: Switzerland is considered a tax haven for investors.
mis.why: False friend! Portuguese "paraíso fiscal" translates to English "tax haven", not "fiscal paradise".

def: Widespread destruction, confusion, or disorder.
ex: A single severe ransomware attack can wreak havoc across a hospital's entire administrative infrastructure.
nat: Unseasonal heavy snowfall wreaked havoc on commuter traffic throughout the metropolitan region yesterday.

mis.bad: The storm made a big havoc in the city.
mis.good: The storm wreaked havoc / caused havoc in the city.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "wreak havoc" (/reɪk ˈhævək/), not "make havoc".

pt: perigo / risco à saúde ou segurança
def: A danger or risk that could cause harm, injury, or loss.
ex: Wearing safety goggles and heavy gloves protects lab technicians against severe chemical hazard risks.
nat: Icy sidewalk conditions pose a serious slip hazard for elderly pedestrians during winter.

mis.bad: Smoking is a big risk for the health.
mis.good: Smoking is a serious health hazard.
mis.why: Use compound noun "health hazard" or "fire hazard" for physical dangers.

def: Risky or dangerous, especially to health or human safety.
ex: Workers wore specialized protective hazmat suits when handling hazardous chemical waste at the recycling plant.
nat: Driving through dense mountain fog and freezing rain is extremely hazardous even with snow chains.

mis.bad: The factory disposed hazardous residues in the river.
mis.good: The factory dumped hazardous waste into the river.
mis.why: Use "hazardous waste" rather than literal translation "hazardous residues".

def: Covered by a haze; misty; or vague and indistinct in memory.
ex: The distant mountain peaks appeared hazy and faint under the warm afternoon summer smog.
nat: I have only a hazy recollection of my family's first apartment in the city.

mis.bad: My memory of that day is very confused.
mis.good: My memory of that day is very hazy / vague.
mis.why: Use "hazy" or "vague" to describe faint or indistinct memories.

def: Loudly vigorous and cheerful; or wholesome and substantial (of food).
ex: After hiking ten miles through the cold rain, we enjoyed a hearty bowl of soup.
nat: The grandfather greeted his visiting grandchildren with a hearty laugh and a warm hug.

mis.bad: We ate a very strong lunch today (meaning substantial).
mis.good: We ate a very hearty / substantial meal today.
mis.why: In English, meals are "hearty" or "substantial", never "strong lunch".

def: Made warm or hot; or passionate and vehement in disagreement.
ex: The architecture committee engaged in a heated debate over whether to adopt microservices architecture.
nat: The resort features an outdoor heated swimming pool open even during snowy winter months.

mis.bad: We had a hot discussion about the budget.
mis.good: We had a heated discussion about the budget.
mis.why: False friend! An angry debate is a "heated discussion" or "heated argument", not "hot discussion".

def: To lift or haul something heavy with great effort; or rise and fall rhythmically.
ex: Together the four warehouse workers managed to heave the heavy iron safe into the truck.
nat: His chest heaved rapidly as he recovered his breath following the four-hundred-meter sprint.

mis.bad: He heaved a sigh of relief when he passed.
mis.good: He breathed a sigh of relief / heaved a sigh of relief.
mis.why: The idiom is "heave a sigh of relief" (dar um suspiro de alívio).

def: Full of incessant or frantic activity; very busy and rushed.
ex: Working at a fast-growing tech startup can be incredibly hectic during end-of-quarter product launches.
nat: After a hectic week of back-to-back customer meetings, she spent Sunday relaxing quietly at home.

mis.bad: My week was very agitated with meetings.
mis.good: My week was very hectic / busy with meetings.
mis.why: False friend! In English, a busy week is "hectic", not "agitated" (which means nervous/irritated).

def: To protect against financial loss by other transactions; or avoid making a direct statement.
ex: Multinational corporations frequently hedge against currency fluctuations using forward foreign exchange derivative contracts.
nat: The politician hedged her answers carefully when questioned about controversial new tax proposals.

mis.bad: We need to hedge about currency risks.
mis.good: We need to hedge against currency risks.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "against" with "hedge": "hedge against risk/inflation".

def: To pay attention to someone's advice, warning, or instructions; take notice of.
ex: Motorists were strongly warned to heed weather warnings and stay off mountain highways tonight.
nat: If he had heeded his doctor's early advice, he might have avoided surgery.

mis.bad: He did not pay heed to the warnings.
mis.good: He did not heed the warnings / pay heed to the warnings.
mis.why: "Heed" is a transitive verb; you can say "heed the warnings" without "to".

def: Large, heavy, and powerful; or impressive in size or monetary amount.
ex: Violating local data protection regulations can result in a hefty fine from European regulators.
nat: The moving crew needed two hefty men to carry the heavy antique oak bookcase.

mis.bad: The company received a heavy fine for pollution.
mis.good: The company received a hefty / heavy fine for pollution.
mis.why: "Hefty fine" is an especially natural, native collocation in business and legal English.

def: To make or become more intense, acute, or prominent.
ex: Recent international cyberattacks have served to heighten security concerns across banking and defense sectors.
nat: Suspense heightened in the cinema as the mystery plot reached its climactic final twist.

mis.bad: The news heightened up the fears of people.
mis.good: The news heightened people's fears.
mis.why: Do not add "up" after "heighten"; the verb already means increase intensity.

def: Of a person or wrongful act, especially a crime: utterly odious or wicked.
ex: The international criminal court prosecuted the former dictator for heinous crimes against innocent civilians.
nat: Kidnapping and human trafficking are universally condemned as heinous offenses against humanity.

mis.bad: He committed an hediond crime.
mis.good: He committed a heinous crime.
mis.why: The English equivalent of Portuguese "hediondo" is "heinous" (/ˈheɪnəs/).

def: A hard or padded protective hat, worn by motorcyclists, cyclists, or construction workers.
ex: City regulations require all electric scooter riders to wear a protective safety helmet outdoors.
nat: Construction workers must keep their hard helmet securely buckled while on the job site.

mis.bad: Put your helmet on your head.
mis.good: Put your helmet on / wear your helmet.
mis.why: Say "put your helmet on" rather than redundant "on your head".

def: Unable to defend oneself or to act without help; powerless.
ex: Volunteers stepped in to protect helpless newborn kittens abandoned outside the animal rescue shelter.
nat: I felt completely helpless watching the database crash without any administrative terminal access.

mis.bad: I felt very non-helpful during the crisis.
mis.good: I felt completely helpless during the crisis.
mis.why: Distinguish "helpless" (powerless) from "unhelpful" (not willing or able to provide assistance).

def: To be a sign that something is about to happen; or announce publicly.
ex: The discovery of quantum supremacy may herald a brand new era in modern scientific computation.
nat: Golden autumn leaves herald the arrival of cooler mountain temperatures across New England.

mis.bad: The innovation heralded to a new era.
mis.good: The innovation heralded a new era.
mis.why: "Herald" is a transitive verb; do not add "to" after it.

def: The passing on of physical or mental characteristics genetically from one generation to another.
ex: Both diet and biological heredity play significant roles in determining long-term cardiovascular health risks.
nat: Mendel conducted pioneering genetic experiments on pea plants to understand the laws of heredity.

mis.bad: Eye color is determined by the hereditability.
mis.good: Eye color is determined by heredity / genetics.
mis.why: Use "heredity" for the general biological passing of traits from parents to offspring.

def: A person admired for courage, outstanding achievements, or noble qualities.
ex: Firefighters who risked their lives to rescue trapped residents were celebrated as local heroes.
nat: Her grandmother has always been her greatest childhood hero and mentor in life.

mis.bad: The firefighters were named as heroes of the city.
mis.good: The firefighters were hailed as heroes of the city.
mis.why: Collocate "hailed as heroes" or "celebrated as heroes".

def: Having the characteristics of a hero or showing extreme courage and bravery.
ex: Volunteers made a heroic effort to rescue stranded villagers during the sudden mountain flash flood.
nat: The doctor performed heroic emergency surgery under difficult blackout conditions in the field hospital.

mis.bad: He made an heroical rescue yesterday.
mis.good: He made a heroic rescue yesterday.
mis.why: The standard English adjective is "heroic", never "heroical".

def: A woman admired for courage or outstanding achievements, or the chief female character.
ex: The courageous young journalist became a national heroine after exposing widespread government financial corruption.
nat: Elizabeth Bennet is the beloved independent heroine of Jane Austen's classic Pride and Prejudice.

mis.bad: She is a heroin of the civil rights movement.
mis.good: She is a heroine of the civil rights movement.
mis.why: Watch the spelling: "heroine" (female hero) has a final "-e"; "heroin" (without -e) is the illegal narcotic drug.

def: The period of a person's or thing's greatest success, popularity, or vigor.
ex: In its nineties heyday, the downtown shopping arcade was filled with thriving luxury boutiques.
nat: During his athletic heyday, the sprinter held three simultaneous Olympic track world records.

mis.bad: The city was in its prime heyday.
mis.good: The city was in its heyday / in its prime.
mis.why: Do not say "prime heyday"; both words denote the peak golden era.

def: Kept out of sight; concealed or secret.
ex: Travelers should always read the fine print carefully to avoid paying unexpected hidden fees.
nat: There is a quiet hidden garden nestled behind the ancient stone church downtown.

mis.bad: The app has many hided costs for users.
mis.good: The app has many hidden costs for users.
mis.why: Irregular past participle: hide — hid — hidden. Never say "hided".

def: Extremely amusing or entertaining; causing loud laughter.
ex: The stand-up comedian delivered a hilarious routine that had the entire theater crying with laughter.
nat: It was hilarious watching the confused kitten try to catch a red laser pointer dot.

mis.bad: The movie was very hilarious to watch.
mis.good: The movie was hilarious / absolutely hilarious to watch.
mis.why: "Hilarious" is an extreme adjective meaning extremely funny; modify with "absolutely", not "very".

pt: girar em torno de / depender crucialmente de
def: To attach with a hinge; or depend entirely on a single condition.
ex: The success of our international expansion will hinge on hiring an experienced regional operations director.
nat: The courtroom trial hinges on whether the digital surveillance footage can be authenticated.

mis.bad: Our future hinges in this decision.
mis.good: Our future hinges on this decision.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "on" (or "upon") after "hinge": "hinge on something".

def: A slight or indirect indication or suggestion; or a small piece of practical advice.
ex: The engineering mentor gave me a helpful hint on how to optimize database queries.
nat: Dark gray clouds on the distant horizon offered the first hint of rain.

mis.bad: Give me a tip hint for the crossword.
mis.good: Give me a hint for the crossword puzzle.
mis.why: Do not say "tip hint"; use "hint" for clues/suggestions or "tip" for practical pointers.

def: To make a sharp sibilant sound as of the letter s, or express disapproval.
ex: Steam began to hiss loudly from the pressure release valve on top of the boiler.
nat: The cornered snake raised its head and hissed aggressively at the approaching dog.

mis.bad: The tea kettle was hissing steam out.
mis.good: The tea kettle was hissing steam.
mis.why: Say "hissing steam" without adding redundant "out".

def: To amass money or valued objects and hide or store them away.
ex: Panicked consumers rushed to hoard bottled water and canned food ahead of the winter blizzard.
nat: Some people tend to hoard old obsolete electronic cables that they never actually use.

mis.bad: He hoarded up all the toilet paper.
mis.good: He hoarded all the toilet paper / stockpiled it.
mis.why: Do not add "up" after "hoard"; "hoard" is directly transitive.

def: Having a hole or empty space inside; or without real significance or value.
ex: The antique wooden dining table was surprisingly light because the legs were completely hollow inside.
nat: Winning the lawsuit felt like a hollow victory after losing their closest business partner.

mis.bad: It was a victory with hollow feeling.
mis.good: It was a hollow victory.
mis.why: Use the classic collocation "hollow victory" (vitória de Pirro / sem valor real).

def: Special honor or respect shown publicly to someone or their artistic work.
ex: The film director paid heartfelt homage to classic Japanese cinema through dramatic black-and-white cinematography.
nat: Musicians gathered at the concert hall to pay homage to the legendary jazz trumpeter.

mis.bad: The band made an homage to the singer.
mis.good: The band paid homage to the singer.
mis.why: The standard collocation in English is "pay homage to someone", not "make an homage".

def: A person's native land or country of origin.
ex: Many international tech immigrants dream of eventually returning to build businesses in their homeland.
nat: Political unrest forced thousands of families to flee their beloved homeland and seek asylum.

mis.bad: He returned to his born country.
mis.good: He returned to his homeland / native country.
mis.why: Say "homeland" or "native country", not "born country".

def: To make uniform or similar; or treat milk so that the fat is evenly distributed.
ex: Globalization can sometimes homogenize urban cultures, making shopping streets look identical across European cities.
nat: Commercial dairy processing plants homogenize fresh milk to prevent cream from separating to the top.

mis.bad: They tried to homegeneize the process.
mis.good: They tried to homogenize the process.
mis.why: Check English spelling: "homogenize" (American) with "-genize", not "-geneize".

def: To regard with great respect; or fulfill an obligation or agreement.
ex: The airline refused to honor the discounted tickets due to an obvious pricing system glitch.
nat: We gathered at the university auditorium to honor our retiring department chair.

mis.bad: The company did not honor with its promise.
mis.good: The company did not honor its promise / commitment.
mis.why: "Honor" is transitive; do not insert "with" when meaning fulfill a contract or promise.

def: Bringing or deserving honor; showing high moral standards.
ex: Resigning immediately after admitting his mistake was widely viewed as an honorable personal decision.
nat: He dedicated thirty honorable years to public education in his underserved rural hometown.

mis.bad: He made an honory decision to leave.
mis.good: He made an honorable decision to leave.
mis.why: The adjective is "honorable" (/ˈɑːnərəbl/), with a silent "h" (use "an honorable").

def: Feeling or inspiring optimism about a future event or situation.
ex: Scientists are hopeful that new vaccine candidates will provide long-lasting immunity against respiratory viruses.
nat: The recent drop in monthly inflation figures is a hopeful sign for the national economy.

mis.bad: I am very hopeful with the new project.
mis.good: I am very hopeful about the new project.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "about" after "hopeful": "hopeful about something".

def: Parallel to the plane of the horizon; at right angles to the vertical.
ex: Hold your mobile smartphone in a horizontal orientation to record widescreen high-definition video.
nat: The architect drew clean horizontal lines across the blueprint to emphasize the low roofline.

mis.bad: Record the video in the horizontal.
mis.good: Record the video horizontally / in landscape mode.
mis.why: Say "horizontally" or "in landscape mode" rather than "in the horizontal".

def: An intense feeling of fear, shock, or disgust; or a genre of fiction.
ex: She watched in horror as the high waves swept the wooden boat toward the rocks.
nat: Many young moviegoers love watching classic psychological horror films in theaters around Halloween.

mis.bad: She looked to the accident with horror.
mis.good: She watched the accident in horror.
mis.why: Use the fixed prepositional phrase "in horror" (em choque/pavor), not "with horror".

def: Friendly and welcoming to strangers or guests; providing favorable conditions.
ex: Local villagers were exceptionally hospitable, inviting our lost hiking group inside for warm herbal tea.
nat: The harsh desert climate is hardly hospitable to delicate agricultural plant varieties.

mis.bad: The people were very hospital with us.
mis.good: The people were very hospitable to us.
mis.why: False friend! "Hospital" is a noun for medical clinics; the adjective for welcoming is "hospitable" (/hɑːˈspɪtəbl/).

def: To act as host at an event; or provide computer server space for a website.
ex: Our company agreed to host the international developer conference at our downtown auditorium next May.
nat: Cloud providers allow developers to host web applications across globally distributed edge servers.

mis.bad: Brazil hosted to the World Cup in 2014.
mis.good: Brazil hosted the World Cup in 2014.
mis.why: "Host" is a transitive verb in English; do not insert "to" after it.

pt: pairar / passar o cursor do mouse
def: To remain in one place in the air; or move mouse cursor over a digital element.
ex: Users can hover over the interactive chart to reveal exact revenue statistics for each quarter.
nat: A rescue helicopter hovered quietly above the stormy ocean while lowering a rescue basket.

mis.bad: Hover your mouse on the button.
mis.good: Hover over the button / hover your mouse over the button.
mis.why: The standard technical collocation in software UI is "hover over [an element]", not "on".

def: To make a long, loud, mournful sound like a dog, or roar with laughter.
ex: Strong arctic winds began to howl through the narrow mountain valleys as darkness fell.
nat: The entire comedy club audience howled with laughter at the comedian's sharp political jokes.

mis.bad: The wind was screaming outside.
mis.good: The wind was howling outside.
mis.why: In English, strong winds "howl", they do not "scream".

def: The effective center of an activity, region, or network; or central airport.
ex: Singapore has long established itself as the leading financial and technological hub of Southeast Asia.
nat: Atlanta operates the world's busiest passenger airline hub with hundreds of connecting daily flights.

mis.bad: The city is a polo of technology.
mis.good: The city is a tech hub / technology hub.
mis.why: False friend! In Portuguese "polo tecnológico" translates to English "tech hub", not "polo".

def: A color or shade; the attribute of a color by virtue of which it is discernible.
ex: The setting autumn sun cast a brilliant golden-orange hue across the calm waters of the bay.
nat: Designers carefully adjusted the color hue on the digital monitor to ensure accurate printing.

mis.bad: The sky had a red color tone (or "tom").
mis.good: The sky had a reddish hue / tint.
mis.why: Use "hue" or "tint" for specific nuanced color shades, rather than "color tone".

def: Marked by a relatively high level of water vapor in the atmosphere.
ex: Summer afternoons in Rio de Janeiro can feel intensely hot and humid for foreign visitors.
nat: Air conditioning units not only cool indoor air but also extract excess humid moisture.

mis.bad: The weather today is very moist.
mis.good: The weather today is very humid.
mis.why: Use "humid" for air/weather; use "moist" for food (cake) or skin.

def: To make someone feel ashamed and foolish by injuring their dignity, especially publicly.
ex: A good engineering manager will never humiliate a junior developer during public pull request reviews.
nat: The basketball champion was careful not to humiliate the outmatched amateur opponents on court.

mis.bad: He humiliated to his colleague in the meeting.
mis.good: He humiliated his colleague in the meeting.
mis.why: "Humiliate" is transitive; do not use "to" before the person.

def: A feeling or guess based on intuition rather than known fact.
ex: Following a strong hunch, the lead detective re-examined the initial timestamp logs on the server.
nat: I have a hunch that our international client will approve the project proposal tomorrow.

mis.bad: I had a palpitation that something went wrong (meaning feeling/hunch).
mis.good: I had a hunch that something had gone wrong.
mis.why: False friend! "Palpitation" refers to rapid heartbeats; for an intuitive guess, use "hunch".

def: An obstacle or difficulty that must be overcome; or a frame jumped in races.
ex: Securing regulatory government approval proved to be the biggest hurdle for the autonomous drone delivery startup.
nat: Athletes leaped gracefully over each hurdle along the straight four-hundred-meter Olympic track.

mis.bad: We passed over the obstacle hurdle.
mis.good: We overcame the hurdle / cleared the hurdle.
mis.why: The natural English verbs with "hurdle" are "overcome a hurdle" or "clear a hurdle".

def: To throw an object with great force; or utter vehement insults at someone.
ex: Angry protesters began to hurl stones and smoke canisters at the protective police barricade.
nat: The frustrated client began to hurl insults at our frontline customer support representative.

mis.bad: He hurled insults to the referee.
mis.good: He hurled insults at the referee.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "at" with "hurl": "hurl insults at someone".

def: To force someone to move hurriedly; or work aggressively to achieve commercial success.
ex: Young entrepreneurs often have to hustle tirelessly every single day to acquire their first hundred customers.
nat: The basketball coach shouted at the players to hustle back on defense after missed shots.

mis.bad: He is making a hustle for money.
mis.good: He is hustling to build his business.
mis.why: Use "hustle" as a verb directly: "hustle to do something". Note silent "t" (/ˈhʌsl/).

def: Of mixed character or composed of mixed parts; combining two different technologies.
ex: Most global technology organizations now operate under a permanent hybrid remote-work policy for engineering staff.
nat: Hybrid electric vehicles combine an internal combustion engine with an electric battery propulsion motor.

mis.bad: We adopt an hybrid system for meetings.
mis.good: We adopt a hybrid system for meetings.
mis.why: The "h" in "hybrid" is pronounced (/ˈhaɪbrɪd/), so use article "a", not "an".

def: Conducive to maintaining health and preventing disease, especially through cleanliness.
ex: Maintaining strictly hygienic kitchen conditions is essential for commercial restaurants to prevent foodborne bacterial contamination.
nat: Stainless steel medical instruments must be kept completely hygienic in sterilized surgical trays.

mis.bad: The restaurant was very clean and hygienical.
mis.good: The restaurant was very clean and hygienic.
mis.why: The standard English adjective is "hygienic", never "hygienical".
